{{Distinguish|Saiin (priestess)}} {{Italic title}} [[File:Saio.jpg|thumb|{{transliteration|ja|Saiō}} in {{transliteration|ja|[[jūnihitoe]]}}, 2007 {{transliteration|ja|[[Saiō Matsuri]]}}]]
{{Nihongo||斎王|'''Saiō'''}} or {{transliteration|ja|'''itsuki no miko'''}}<ref>{{cite book|title=スーパー大辞林|trans-title=Super [[Daijirin]]}}</ref> was the title of the unmarried female members of the [[Imperial House of Japan|Japanese Imperial Family]], sent to serve at [[Ise Grand Shrine]] from the late 7th century to the 14th century. The {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}'s residence, {{Nihongo|[[Saikū]]|斎宮}}, was about {{cvt|10|km}} north-west of the shrine. The remains of Saikū are situated in the town of [[Meiwa, Mie|Meiwa]], [[Mie Prefecture]], [[Japan]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.bunka.pref.mie.lg.jp/saiku/p0048200012.htm|title = 斎宮歴史博物館 Reduced-scale reconstruction of the Saikuryo}}</ref>
== Origins == [[File:Saio genji.jpg|thumb|left|image from the ''[[Tale of Genji]]'' showing what life at Saikū might have been like]]
According to Japanese legend, around 2,000 years ago the divine [[Yamatohime-no-mikoto]], daughter of the [[Emperor Suinin]], set out from [[Mount Miwa]] in [[Nara Prefecture]] in search of a permanent location to worship the goddess [[Amaterasu|Amaterasu-ōmikami]].<ref>Brown Delmer ''et al.'' (1979). ''Gukanshō'', p. 253; Varley, H. Paul. (1980). ''Jinnō Shōtōki,'' pp. 95-96; [https://books.google.com/books?id=18oNAAAAIAAJ&pg=PP9&dq=nipon+o+dai+itsi+ran#PRA1-PA10,M1 Titsingh, Isaac. (1834). ''Annales des empereurs du japon,'' p. 10].</ref> Her search lasted for 20 years and eventually brought her to Ise, Mie Prefecture, where the Ise Shrine now stands.<ref>''The Deep Purple Story of Meiwa (紫紺の語り部)'' (Meiwa Town Office, 2003), p. 3.</ref> Prior to Yamatohime-no-mikoto's journey, Amaterasu-ōmikami had been worshiped at the Imperial Palaces in [[Yamato Province|Yamato]].
According to the {{transliteration|ja|[[Man'yōshū]]}} (''The Anthology of Ten Thousand Leaves''), the first {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} to serve at Ise was [[Princess Ōku]], daughter of [[Emperor Tenmu]], during the [[:en:Asuka period|Asuka period]] of Japanese history. Mention of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} is also made in the {{transliteration|ja|Aoi}}, {{transliteration|ja|Sakaki}} and {{transliteration|ja|Yugao}} chapters of ''[[The Tale of Genji]]'', as well as in the 69th chapter of ''[[The Tales of Ise]]'' ({{transliteration|ja|Ise Monogatari}}).
In the 13th century, [[Jien]] recorded in the {{transliteration|ja|[[Gukanshō]]}} that during the reign of Emperor Suinin, the first High Priestess ({{transliteration|ja|saiō}}) was appointed for Ise Shrine.<ref>Brown, p. 253.</ref> [[Hayashi Gahō]]'s 17th-century {{transliteration|ja|[[Nihon Ōdai Ichiran]]}} is somewhat more expansive, explaining that since Suinin's time, a daughter of the emperor was almost always appointed as high priestess, but across the centuries, there had been times when the emperor himself had no daughter; and in such circumstances, the daughter of a close relative of the emperor would have been appointed to fill the untimely vacancy.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=18oNAAAAIAAJ&pg=PP9&dq=nipon+o+dai+itsi+ran#PRA1-PA9,M1 Titsingh, p. 10].</ref>
== Role == [[File:Saikū Historical Museum - Display item05 - The room of Saiô.jpg|thumb|Recreation of the room of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}, in the Saikū Historical Museum]]
The role of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} was to serve as High Priestess at Ise Shrine on behalf of the Emperor, to represent the role first set out by Yamatohime-no-mikoto. Three rituals a year were conducted at the Shrine in which the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} prayed for peace and protection. In June and November each year, she journeyed to the Shrine to perform the Tsukinamisai Festival. In September in the [[lunisolar calendar]], she performed the [[Kannamesai Festival]] to make offerings to the {{transliteration|ja|[[kami]]}} of the year's new grain harvest.<ref name="m9">''The Deep Purple Story of Meiwa'', p. 9.</ref>
For the rest of the year, the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} lived in [[Saikū]], a small town of up to 500 people approximately {{cvt|10|km}} north-west of Ise, in modern Meiwa, Mie Prefecture. Life at Saikū was, for the most part, peaceful. The {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} would spend her time composing {{transliteration|ja|[[waka (poetry)|waka]]}} verses, collect shells on the shore of Ōyodo beach, or set out in boats and recite poetry upon the water and wait to be recalled to [[Kyoto]].<ref name="m9"/>
== Selection process == When an Emperor died or abdicated the throne, when the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}'s relative died, or when certain political power required, she would be recalled to the capital and a new {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} selected from one of the new Emperor's unmarried female relatives using divination by either burnt tortoise shell or deer bones. The new {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} would then undergo a period of purification before setting out with her retinue of up to 500 people for Saikū, never to return to the capital until recalled by the next Emperor.
Upon the selection of the new {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}, the current {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} and her retinue would return to the capital to resume their lives as part of the Imperial Court. Often, a {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} was quite young when she left the capital for Saikū, and would only be in her mid-teens or early twenties when she returned to the capital. It was considered a great honor to marry a former {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} and her time at Saikū improved her own position at court and those of the people who served with her.
== Procession to Saikū == [[File:Saiku map.jpg|thumb|Map of the travel routes to Saikū, the seat of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}]] [[File:Tarumitongu.jpg|thumb|The Tarumi-tongū temporary residence]] The procession routes of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} changed after the capital was moved to [[Heian-kyō]] in 794.
The procession began in what is today the Arashiyama district on the west side of Kyoto. In the Heian period, successive imperial princesses stayed in the [[Nonomiya Shrine]] for a year or more to purify themselves before becoming representatives of the imperial family at the Ise Shrine.<ref>Kyoto City Tourism and Culture Information Site: [http://kaiwai.city.kyoto.jp/raku/backnum/dec07_e/buttone3.html Nonomiya Shrine.] {{webarchive|url=https://archive.today/20070626055413/http://kaiwai.city.kyoto.jp/raku/backnum/dec07_e/buttone3.html |date=2007-06-26 }}</ref> Contemporary annual processions recreate a scene from a picture scroll of the imperial court during the Heian period, starting from the shrine and continuing as far as the Togetsu-kyo Bridge, Arashiyama.<ref>Kyoto City: [http://kaiwai.city.kyoto.jp/raku/backnum/nov08_e/gyoji_dtle.html Saigū Procession];{{dead link|date=May 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} [http://raku.city.kyoto.jp/backnum/oct06_e/oct06_topics_e.html Events, October 2006.]{{dead link|date=May 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>
The procession of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} from [[Kyoto]] to [[Saikū]], the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}'s official residence in [[Ise, Mie|Ise]], was the largest procession of its kind in Japan for its time. Up to 500 people would set out from Kyoto as a part of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}'s retinue for the journey, which lasted six days and five nights. From Kyoto, they travelled in an eastward direction, passing through the [[Suzuka, Mie|Suzuka]] Pass, which was without doubt the most difficult part of the journey. Once clearing the pass, the retinue would descend into the Ise region and turn south, eventually reaching the {{nihongo|Kushida River|櫛田川}}. Here, the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} would stop to perform a final cleansing ritual before crossing the river and travelling the short distance to Saikū.<ref>''Saiō Procession'' (Documentary movie, Saikū Historical Museum).</ref>
The {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} was expected to remain at Saikū until the emperor whom she represented either died or abdicated the throne. The {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} was permitted to return to Kyoto only on the provision of a close relative's death. When returning to Kyoto, a different route was taken through the mountains to Nara, then to Osaka Bay where a ceremony was to be performed before she could finally return to the capital.
==From Japanese literature==
===Princess Ōku=== The {{transliteration|ja|[[Man'yōshū]]}} (''The Anthology of Ten Thousand Leaves''), tells the story of [[Princess Ōku]], the first {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} to serve at [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Shrine]]. The daughter of [[Emperor Tenmu]], Japan's 40th emperor (according to the traditional order of succession), Princess Ōku and her younger brother, [[Prince Ōtsu]], survived the [[Jinshin incident]]. After taking up her role as {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}, her brother was put to death for treason in 686 and Princess Ōku was relieved of her duties and returned to Yamato. Here, she enshrined her brother's remains on Mt. Futakami before she died the age of 41.<ref name="m6">''The Deep Purple Story of Meiwa'', p. 6.</ref>
===Princess Yoshiko=== ''[[The Tale of Genji]]'' tells the story of Rokujo-no-miyasudokoro, which is believed to be based on Princess Yoshiko, who served as {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} from 936 to 945. In ''The Tale of Genji'', Rokujo-no-miyasudokoro became the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} of Ise Shrine at the young age of 8, serving at the shrine for 9 years. After returning to the capital, she became a consort to [[Emperor Murakami]] and gave birth to Princess Noriko. She became famous throughout Kyoto for her colorful life, devoting herself to waka poetry and music. According to the story, she falls in love with Prince Genji, but her jealous nature brings about the death of two of her rivals. When her daughter is chosen as {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} at the age of 13, Rokujo-no-miyasudokoro decides to join her in Saikū to help her overcome her feelings for Genji.<ref name="m6"/>
===Princess Yasuko=== The love story of [[:en:Ariwara no Narihira|Ariwara-no-Narihira]] and the 31st {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}, Princess Yasuko (served as {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} from 859 to 876), is told in the 69th chapter of ''The Tales of Ise''. Ariwara-no-Narihira, well known in his time for his good looks, is married to Princess Yasuko's cousin, but on meeting at the Saikū, they fall into forbidden love. Giving in to temptation, they secretly meet under a pine tree on the shore of Ōyodo Port to reveal their feelings for one another and to promise to meet again the following night. But this first secret meeting would also be the last, as Narihira was due to depart that next day for [[Owari Province]]. Princess Yasuko came to see Narihira off, and they were never to see each other again, though it is said that Princess Yasuko bore a child as a result of the brief love affair.<ref>''The Deep Purple Story of Meiwa'', p. 5.</ref>
==End of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} system== It is not precisely clear when the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} system ended, but what is known is that it occurred during the turmoil of the [[Nanboku-chō period]] when two rival Imperial courts were in existence, in Kyoto and [[Yoshino, Nara|Yoshino]]. The {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} system had been in steady decline up to this period, with Saikū reverting to just another rural rice farming village after the system's collapse.
Though the area of Saikū remained, it was unclear exactly where the old Imperial town stood until pottery remains were unearthed in 1970 during the construction of housing in the Saikū area, Meiwa Town. A modern museum was built on the site of the first finds and archaeological excavations are continuing, held each summer with the aid of volunteer school children from all over Japan. Though a site for the main {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} residence has been discovered, a large percentage of it lies beneath the main [[Kintetsu Railway|Kintetsu]] Ise railway line and is inaccessible. Itsukinomiya Historical Experience Hall, a reconstruction of the building using traditional techniques, was built in the 1990s and stands beside Saikū station on the local Kintetsu rail line, no more than {{convert|200|m}} from the original site.
==Festivals== [[File:SaioMatsuri.jpg|thumb|The 2007 {{transliteration|ja|Saiō Matsuri}} in Meiwa, Mie Prefecture]] The {{transliteration|ja|[[Aoi Matsuri]]}}, the first of the three main festivals held in Kyoto each year, re-enacts the [[Heian period]] march of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} to the Shimigamo Shrine (lower [[Kamo shrines|Kamo Shrine]]) in Sakyo Ward. This festival is held every year on May 15 and in 2006 consisted of 511 people dressed in traditional Heian court clothing and 40 cows and horses, stretching around {{cvt|800|m}} from start to finish. This festival is said to have started in the 6th century when the Emperor sent his representatives to Shimogamo and Kamigamo Shines to pray from good harvests.
The {{transliteration|ja|[[Saiō Matsuri]]}} is held in the town of Meiwa, Mie Prefecture, on the first weekend of June each year. First held in 1983, it re-enacts the march of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} from her residence at Saikū, to the nearby Ise Shrine. More than 100 people dressed in traditional Heian-period dress along a section of the old Ise {{transliteration|ja|kaido}} (pilgrimage road), before ending in the grounds of the Saikū Museum.

{{Distinguish|Saiin (priestess)}} {{Italic title}} [[File:Saio.jpg|thumb|{{transliteration|ja|Saiō}} in {{transliteration|ja|[[jūnihitoe]]}}, 2007 {{transliteration|ja|[[Saiō Matsuri]]}}]]
{{Nihongo||斎王|'''Saiō'''}} or {{transliteration|ja|'''itsuki no miko'''}}<ref>{{cite book|title=スーパー大辞林|trans-title=Super [[Daijirin]]}}</ref> was the title of the unmarried female members of the [[Imperial House of Japan|Japanese Imperial Family]], sent to serve at [[Ise Grand Shrine]] from the late 7th century to the 14th century. The {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}'s residence, {{Nihongo|[[Saikū]]|斎宮}}, was about {{cvt|10|km}} north-west of the shrine. The remains of Saikū are situated in the town of [[Meiwa, Mie|Meiwa]], [[Mie Prefecture]], [[Japan]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.bunka.pref.mie.lg.jp/saiku/p0048200012.htm|title = 斎宮歴史博物館 Reduced-scale reconstruction of the Saikuryo}}</ref>
== Origins == [[File:Saio genji.jpg|thumb|left|image from the ''[[Tale of Genji]]'' showing what life at Saikū might have been like]]
According to Japanese legend, around 2,000 years ago the divine [[Yamatohime-no-mikoto]], daughter of the [[Emperor Suinin]], set out from [[Mount Miwa]] in [[Nara Prefecture]] in search of a permanent location to worship the goddess [[Amaterasu|Amaterasu-ōmikami]].<ref>Brown Delmer ''et al.'' (1979). ''Gukanshō'', p. 253; Varley, H. Paul. (1980). ''Jinnō Shōtōki,'' pp. 95-96; [https://books.google.com/books?id=18oNAAAAIAAJ&pg=PP9&dq=nipon+o+dai+itsi+ran#PRA1-PA10,M1 Titsingh, Isaac. (1834). ''Annales des empereurs du japon,'' p. 10].</ref> Her search lasted for 20 years and eventually brought her to Ise, Mie Prefecture, where the Ise Shrine now stands.<ref>''The Deep Purple Story of Meiwa (紫紺の語り部)'' (Meiwa Town Office, 2003), p. 3.</ref> Prior to Yamatohime-no-mikoto's journey, Amaterasu-ōmikami had been worshiped at the Imperial Palaces in [[Yamato Province|Yamato]].
According to the {{transliteration|ja|[[Man'yōshū]]}} (''The Anthology of Ten Thousand Leaves''), the first {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} to serve at Ise was [[Princess Ōku]], daughter of [[Emperor Tenmu]], during the [[:en:Asuka period|Asuka period]] of Japanese history. Mention of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} is also made in the {{transliteration|ja|Aoi}}, {{transliteration|ja|Sakaki}} and {{transliteration|ja|Yugao}} chapters of ''[[The Tale of Genji]]'', as well as in the 69th chapter of ''[[The Tales of Ise]]'' ({{transliteration|ja|Ise Monogatari}}).
In the 13th century, [[Jien]] recorded in the {{transliteration|ja|[[Gukanshō]]}} that during the reign of Emperor Suinin, the first High Priestess ({{transliteration|ja|saiō}}) was appointed for Ise Shrine.<ref>Brown, p. 253.</ref> [[Hayashi Gahō]]'s 17th-century {{transliteration|ja|[[Nihon Ōdai Ichiran]]}} is somewhat more expansive, explaining that since Suinin's time, a daughter of the emperor was almost always appointed as high priestess, but across the centuries, there had been times when the emperor himself had no daughter; and in such circumstances, the daughter of a close relative of the emperor would have been appointed to fill the untimely vacancy.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=18oNAAAAIAAJ&pg=PP9&dq=nipon+o+dai+itsi+ran#PRA1-PA9,M1 Titsingh, p. 10].</ref>
== Role == [[File:Saikū Historical Museum - Display item05 - The room of Saiô.jpg|thumb|Recreation of the room of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}, in the Saikū Historical Museum]]
The role of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} was to serve as High Priestess at Ise Shrine on behalf of the Emperor, to represent the role first set out by Yamatohime-no-mikoto. Three rituals a year were conducted at the Shrine in which the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} prayed for peace and protection. In June and November each year, she journeyed to the Shrine to perform the Tsukinamisai Festival. In September in the [[lunisolar calendar]], she performed the [[Kannamesai Festival]] to make offerings to the {{transliteration|ja|[[kami]]}} of the year's new grain harvest.<ref name="m9">''The Deep Purple Story of Meiwa'', p. 9.</ref>
For the rest of the year, the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} lived in [[Saikū]], a small town of up to 500 people approximately {{cvt|10|km}} north-west of Ise, in modern Meiwa, Mie Prefecture. Life at Saikū was, for the most part, peaceful. The {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} would spend her time composing {{transliteration|ja|[[waka (poetry)|waka]]}} verses, collect shells on the shore of Ōyodo beach, or set out in boats and recite poetry upon the water and wait to be recalled to [[Kyoto]].<ref name="m9"/>
== Selection process == When an Emperor died or abdicated the throne, when the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}'s relative died, or when certain political power required, she would be recalled to the capital and a new {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} selected from one of the new Emperor's unmarried female relatives using divination by either burnt tortoise shell or deer bones. The new {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} would then undergo a period of purification before setting out with her retinue of up to 500 people for Saikū, never to return to the capital until recalled by the next Emperor.
Upon the selection of the new {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}, the current {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} and her retinue would return to the capital to resume their lives as part of the Imperial Court. Often, a {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} was quite young when she left the capital for Saikū, and would only be in her mid-teens or early twenties when she returned to the capital. It was considered a great honor to marry a former {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} and her time at Saikū improved her own position at court and those of the people who served with her.
== Procession to Saikū == [[File:Saiku map.jpg|thumb|Map of the travel routes to Saikū, the seat of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}]] [[File:Tarumitongu.jpg|thumb|The Tarumi-tongū temporary residence]] The procession routes of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} changed after the capital was moved to [[Heian-kyō]] in 794.
The procession began in what is today the Arashiyama district on the west side of Kyoto. In the Heian period, successive imperial princesses stayed in the [[Nonomiya Shrine]] for a year or more to purify themselves before becoming representatives of the imperial family at the Ise Shrine.<ref>Kyoto City Tourism and Culture Information Site: [http://kaiwai.city.kyoto.jp/raku/backnum/dec07_e/buttone3.html Nonomiya Shrine.] {{webarchive|url=https://archive.today/20070626055413/http://kaiwai.city.kyoto.jp/raku/backnum/dec07_e/buttone3.html |date=2007-06-26 }}</ref> Contemporary annual processions recreate a scene from a picture scroll of the imperial court during the Heian period, starting from the shrine and continuing as far as the Togetsu-kyo Bridge, Arashiyama.<ref>Kyoto City: [http://kaiwai.city.kyoto.jp/raku/backnum/nov08_e/gyoji_dtle.html Saigū Procession];{{dead link|date=May 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} [http://raku.city.kyoto.jp/backnum/oct06_e/oct06_topics_e.html Events, October 2006.]{{dead link|date=May 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>
The procession of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} from [[Kyoto]] to [[Saikū]], the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}'s official residence in [[Ise, Mie|Ise]], was the largest procession of its kind in Japan for its time. Up to 500 people would set out from Kyoto as a part of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}'s retinue for the journey, which lasted six days and five nights. From Kyoto, they travelled in an eastward direction, passing through the [[Suzuka, Mie|Suzuka]] Pass, which was without doubt the most difficult part of the journey. Once clearing the pass, the retinue would descend into the Ise region and turn south, eventually reaching the {{nihongo|Kushida River|櫛田川}}. Here, the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} would stop to perform a final cleansing ritual before crossing the river and travelling the short distance to Saikū.<ref>''Saiō Procession'' (Documentary movie, Saikū Historical Museum).</ref>
The {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} was expected to remain at Saikū until the emperor whom she represented either died or abdicated the throne. The {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} was permitted to return to Kyoto only on the provision of a close relative's death. When returning to Kyoto, a different route was taken through the mountains to Nara, then to Osaka Bay where a ceremony was to be performed before she could finally return to the capital.
==From Japanese literature==
===Princess Ōku=== The {{transliteration|ja|[[Man'yōshū]]}} (''The Anthology of Ten Thousand Leaves''), tells the story of [[Princess Ōku]], the first {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} to serve at [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Shrine]]. The daughter of [[Emperor Tenmu]], Japan's 40th emperor (according to the traditional order of succession), Princess Ōku and her younger brother, [[Prince Ōtsu]], survived the [[Jinshin incident]]. After taking up her role as {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}, her brother was put to death for treason in 686 and Princess Ōku was relieved of her duties and returned to Yamato. Here, she enshrined her brother's remains on Mt. Futakami before she died the age of 41.<ref name="m6">''The Deep Purple Story of Meiwa'', p. 6.</ref>
===Princess Yoshiko=== ''[[The Tale of Genji]]'' tells the story of Rokujo-no-miyasudokoro, which is believed to be based on Princess Yoshiko, who served as {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} from 936 to 945. In ''The Tale of Genji'', Rokujo-no-miyasudokoro became the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} of Ise Shrine at the young age of 8, serving at the shrine for 9 years. After returning to the capital, she became a consort to [[Emperor Murakami]] and gave birth to Princess Noriko. She became famous throughout Kyoto for her colorful life, devoting herself to waka poetry and music. According to the story, she falls in love with Prince Genji, but her jealous nature brings about the death of two of her rivals. When her daughter is chosen as {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} at the age of 13, Rokujo-no-miyasudokoro decides to join her in Saikū to help her overcome her feelings for Genji.<ref name="m6"/>
===Princess Yasuko=== The love story of [[:en:Ariwara no Narihira|Ariwara-no-Narihira]] and the 31st {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}, Princess Yasuko (served as {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} from 859 to 876), is told in the 69th chapter of ''The Tales of Ise''. Ariwara-no-Narihira, well known in his time for his good looks, is married to Princess Yasuko's cousin, but on meeting at the Saikū, they fall into forbidden love. Giving in to temptation, they secretly meet under a pine tree on the shore of Ōyodo Port to reveal their feelings for one another and to promise to meet again the following night. But this first secret meeting would also be the last, as Narihira was due to depart that next day for [[Owari Province]]. Princess Yasuko came to see Narihira off, and they were never to see each other again, though it is said that Princess Yasuko bore a child as a result of the brief love affair.<ref>''The Deep Purple Story of Meiwa'', p. 5.</ref>
==End of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} system== It is not precisely clear when the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} system ended, but what is known is that it occurred during the turmoil of the [[Nanboku-chō period]] when two rival Imperial courts were in existence, in Kyoto and [[Yoshino, Nara|Yoshino]]. The {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} system had been in steady decline up to this period, with Saikū reverting to just another rural rice farming village after the system's collapse.
Though the area of Saikū remained, it was unclear exactly where the old Imperial town stood until pottery remains were unearthed in 1970 during the construction of housing in the Saikū area, Meiwa Town. A modern museum was built on the site of the first finds and archaeological excavations are continuing, held each summer with the aid of volunteer school children from all over Japan. Though a site for the main {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} residence has been discovered, a large percentage of it lies beneath the main [[Kintetsu Railway|Kintetsu]] Ise railway line and is inaccessible. Itsukinomiya Historical Experience Hall, a reconstruction of the building using traditional techniques, was built in the 1990s and stands beside Saikū station on the local Kintetsu rail line, no more than {{convert|200|m}} from the original site.
==Festivals== [[File:SaioMatsuri.jpg|thumb|The 2007 {{transliteration|ja|Saiō Matsuri}} in Meiwa, Mie Prefecture]] The {{transliteration|ja|[[Aoi Matsuri]]}}, the first of the three main festivals held in Kyoto each year, re-enacts the [[Heian period]] march of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} to the Shimigamo Shrine (lower [[Kamo shrines|Kamo Shrine]]) in Sakyo Ward. This festival is held every year on May 15 and in 2006 consisted of 511 people dressed in traditional Heian court clothing and 40 cows and horses, stretching around {{cvt|800|m}} from start to finish. This festival is said to have started in the 6th century when the Emperor sent his representatives to Shimogamo and Kamigamo Shines to pray from good harvests.
The {{transliteration|ja|[[Saiō Matsuri]]}} is held in the town of Meiwa, Mie Prefecture, on the first weekend of June each year. First held in 1983, it re-enacts the march of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} from her residence at Saikū, to the nearby Ise Shrine. More than 100 people dressed in traditional Heian-period dress along a section of the old Ise {{transliteration|ja|kaido}} (pilgrimage road), before ending in the grounds of the Saikū Museum.

{{Distinguish|Saiin (priestess)}} {{Italic title}} [[File:Saio.jpg|thumb|{{transliteration|ja|Saiō}} in {{transliteration|ja|[[jūnihitoe]]}}, 2007 {{transliteration|ja|[[Saiō Matsuri]]}}]]
{{Nihongo||斎王|'''Saiō'''}} or {{transliteration|ja|'''itsuki no miko'''}}<ref>{{cite book|title=スーパー大辞林|trans-title=Super [[Daijirin]]}}</ref> was the title of the unmarried female members of the [[Imperial House of Japan|Japanese Imperial Family]], sent to serve at [[Ise Grand Shrine]] from the late 7th century to the 14th century. The {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}'s residence, {{Nihongo|[[Saikū]]|斎宮}}, was about {{cvt|10|km}} north-west of the shrine. The remains of Saikū are situated in the town of [[Meiwa, Mie|Meiwa]], [[Mie Prefecture]], [[Japan]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.bunka.pref.mie.lg.jp/saiku/p0048200012.htm|title = 斎宮歴史博物館 Reduced-scale reconstruction of the Saikuryo}}</ref>
== Origins == [[File:Saio genji.jpg|thumb|left|image from the ''[[Tale of Genji]]'' showing what life at Saikū might have been like]]
According to Japanese legend, around 2,000 years ago the divine [[Yamatohime-no-mikoto]], daughter of the [[Emperor Suinin]], set out from [[Mount Miwa]] in [[Nara Prefecture]] in search of a permanent location to worship the goddess [[Amaterasu|Amaterasu-ōmikami]].<ref>Brown Delmer ''et al.'' (1979). ''Gukanshō'', p. 253; Varley, H. Paul. (1980). ''Jinnō Shōtōki,'' pp. 95-96; [https://books.google.com/books?id=18oNAAAAIAAJ&pg=PP9&dq=nipon+o+dai+itsi+ran#PRA1-PA10,M1 Titsingh, Isaac. (1834). ''Annales des empereurs du japon,'' p. 10].</ref> Her search lasted for 20 years and eventually brought her to Ise, Mie Prefecture, where the Ise Shrine now stands.<ref>''The Deep Purple Story of Meiwa (紫紺の語り部)'' (Meiwa Town Office, 2003), p. 3.</ref> Prior to Yamatohime-no-mikoto's journey, Amaterasu-ōmikami had been worshiped at the Imperial Palaces in [[Yamato Province|Yamato]].
According to the {{transliteration|ja|[[Man'yōshū]]}} (''The Anthology of Ten Thousand Leaves''), the first {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} to serve at Ise was [[Princess Ōku]], daughter of [[Emperor Tenmu]], during the [[:en:Asuka period|Asuka period]] of Japanese history. Mention of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} is also made in the {{transliteration|ja|Aoi}}, {{transliteration|ja|Sakaki}} and {{transliteration|ja|Yugao}} chapters of ''[[The Tale of Genji]]'', as well as in the 69th chapter of ''[[The Tales of Ise]]'' ({{transliteration|ja|Ise Monogatari}}).
In the 13th century, [[Jien]] recorded in the {{transliteration|ja|[[Gukanshō]]}} that during the reign of Emperor Suinin, the first High Priestess ({{transliteration|ja|saiō}}) was appointed for Ise Shrine.<ref>Brown, p. 253.</ref> [[Hayashi Gahō]]'s 17th-century {{transliteration|ja|[[Nihon Ōdai Ichiran]]}} is somewhat more expansive, explaining that since Suinin's time, a daughter of the emperor was almost always appointed as high priestess, but across the centuries, there had been times when the emperor himself had no daughter; and in such circumstances, the daughter of a close relative of the emperor would have been appointed to fill the untimely vacancy.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=18oNAAAAIAAJ&pg=PP9&dq=nipon+o+dai+itsi+ran#PRA1-PA9,M1 Titsingh, p. 10].</ref>
== Role == [[File:Saikū Historical Museum - Display item05 - The room of Saiô.jpg|thumb|Recreation of the room of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}, in the Saikū Historical Museum]]
The role of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} was to serve as High Priestess at Ise Shrine on behalf of the Emperor, to represent the role first set out by Yamatohime-no-mikoto. Three rituals a year were conducted at the Shrine in which the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} prayed for peace and protection. In June and November each year, she journeyed to the Shrine to perform the Tsukinamisai Festival. In September in the [[lunisolar calendar]], she performed the [[Kannamesai Festival]] to make offerings to the {{transliteration|ja|[[kami]]}} of the year's new grain harvest.<ref name="m9">''The Deep Purple Story of Meiwa'', p. 9.</ref>
For the rest of the year, the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} lived in [[Saikū]], a small town of up to 500 people approximately {{cvt|10|km}} north-west of Ise, in modern Meiwa, Mie Prefecture. Life at Saikū was, for the most part, peaceful. The {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} would spend her time composing {{transliteration|ja|[[waka (poetry)|waka]]}} verses, collect shells on the shore of Ōyodo beach, or set out in boats and recite poetry upon the water and wait to be recalled to [[Kyoto]].<ref name="m9"/>
== Selection process == When an Emperor died or abdicated the throne, when the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}'s relative died, or when certain political power required, she would be recalled to the capital and a new {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} selected from one of the new Emperor's unmarried female relatives using divination by either burnt tortoise shell or deer bones. The new {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} would then undergo a period of purification before setting out with her retinue of up to 500 people for Saikū, never to return to the capital until recalled by the next Emperor.
Upon the selection of the new {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}, the current {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} and her retinue would return to the capital to resume their lives as part of the Imperial Court. Often, a {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} was quite young when she left the capital for Saikū, and would only be in her mid-teens or early twenties when she returned to the capital. It was considered a great honor to marry a former {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} and her time at Saikū improved her own position at court and those of the people who served with her.
== Procession to Saikū == [[File:Saiku map.jpg|thumb|Map of the travel routes to Saikū, the seat of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}]] [[File:Tarumitongu.jpg|thumb|The Tarumi-tongū temporary residence]] The procession routes of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} changed after the capital was moved to [[Heian-kyō]] in 794.
The procession began in what is today the Arashiyama district on the west side of Kyoto. In the Heian period, successive imperial princesses stayed in the [[Nonomiya Shrine]] for a year or more to purify themselves before becoming representatives of the imperial family at the Ise Shrine.<ref>Kyoto City Tourism and Culture Information Site: [http://kaiwai.city.kyoto.jp/raku/backnum/dec07_e/buttone3.html Nonomiya Shrine.] {{webarchive|url=https://archive.today/20070626055413/http://kaiwai.city.kyoto.jp/raku/backnum/dec07_e/buttone3.html |date=2007-06-26 }}</ref> Contemporary annual processions recreate a scene from a picture scroll of the imperial court during the Heian period, starting from the shrine and continuing as far as the Togetsu-kyo Bridge, Arashiyama.<ref>Kyoto City: [http://kaiwai.city.kyoto.jp/raku/backnum/nov08_e/gyoji_dtle.html Saigū Procession];{{dead link|date=May 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} [http://raku.city.kyoto.jp/backnum/oct06_e/oct06_topics_e.html Events, October 2006.]{{dead link|date=May 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>
The procession of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} from [[Kyoto]] to [[Saikū]], the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}'s official residence in [[Ise, Mie|Ise]], was the largest procession of its kind in Japan for its time. Up to 500 people would set out from Kyoto as a part of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}'s retinue for the journey, which lasted six days and five nights. From Kyoto, they travelled in an eastward direction, passing through the [[Suzuka, Mie|Suzuka]] Pass, which was without doubt the most difficult part of the journey. Once clearing the pass, the retinue would descend into the Ise region and turn south, eventually reaching the {{nihongo|Kushida River|櫛田川}}. Here, the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} would stop to perform a final cleansing ritual before crossing the river and travelling the short distance to Saikū.<ref>''Saiō Procession'' (Documentary movie, Saikū Historical Museum).</ref>
The {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} was expected to remain at Saikū until the emperor whom she represented either died or abdicated the throne. The {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} was permitted to return to Kyoto only on the provision of a close relative's death. When returning to Kyoto, a different route was taken through the mountains to Nara, then to Osaka Bay where a ceremony was to be performed before she could finally return to the capital.
==From Japanese literature==
===Princess Ōku=== The {{transliteration|ja|[[Man'yōshū]]}} (''The Anthology of Ten Thousand Leaves''), tells the story of [[Princess Ōku]], the first {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} to serve at [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Shrine]]. The daughter of [[Emperor Tenmu]], Japan's 40th emperor (according to the traditional order of succession), Princess Ōku and her younger brother, [[Prince Ōtsu]], survived the [[Jinshin incident]]. After taking up her role as {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}, her brother was put to death for treason in 686 and Princess Ōku was relieved of her duties and returned to Yamato. Here, she enshrined her brother's remains on Mt. Futakami before she died the age of 41.<ref name="m6">''The Deep Purple Story of Meiwa'', p. 6.</ref>
===Princess Yoshiko=== ''[[The Tale of Genji]]'' tells the story of Rokujo-no-miyasudokoro, which is believed to be based on Princess Yoshiko, who served as {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} from 936 to 945. In ''The Tale of Genji'', Rokujo-no-miyasudokoro became the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} of Ise Shrine at the young age of 8, serving at the shrine for 9 years. After returning to the capital, she became a consort to [[Emperor Murakami]] and gave birth to Princess Noriko. She became famous throughout Kyoto for her colorful life, devoting herself to waka poetry and music. According to the story, she falls in love with Prince Genji, but her jealous nature brings about the death of two of her rivals. When her daughter is chosen as {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} at the age of 13, Rokujo-no-miyasudokoro decides to join her in Saikū to help her overcome her feelings for Genji.<ref name="m6"/>
===Princess Yasuko=== The love story of [[:en:Ariwara no Narihira|Ariwara-no-Narihira]] and the 31st {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}, Princess Yasuko (served as {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} from 859 to 876), is told in the 69th chapter of ''The Tales of Ise''. Ariwara-no-Narihira, well known in his time for his good looks, is married to Princess Yasuko's cousin, but on meeting at the Saikū, they fall into forbidden love. Giving in to temptation, they secretly meet under a pine tree on the shore of Ōyodo Port to reveal their feelings for one another and to promise to meet again the following night. But this first secret meeting would also be the last, as Narihira was due to depart that next day for [[Owari Province]]. Princess Yasuko came to see Narihira off, and they were never to see each other again, though it is said that Princess Yasuko bore a child as a result of the brief love affair.<ref>''The Deep Purple Story of Meiwa'', p. 5.</ref>
==End of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} system== It is not precisely clear when the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} system ended, but what is known is that it occurred during the turmoil of the [[Nanboku-chō period]] when two rival Imperial courts were in existence, in Kyoto and [[Yoshino, Nara|Yoshino]]. The {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} system had been in steady decline up to this period, with Saikū reverting to just another rural rice farming village after the system's collapse.
Though the area of Saikū remained, it was unclear exactly where the old Imperial town stood until pottery remains were unearthed in 1970 during the construction of housing in the Saikū area, Meiwa Town. A modern museum was built on the site of the first finds and archaeological excavations are continuing, held each summer with the aid of volunteer school children from all over Japan. Though a site for the main {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} residence has been discovered, a large percentage of it lies beneath the main [[Kintetsu Railway|Kintetsu]] Ise railway line and is inaccessible. Itsukinomiya Historical Experience Hall, a reconstruction of the building using traditional techniques, was built in the 1990s and stands beside Saikū station on the local Kintetsu rail line, no more than {{convert|200|m}} from the original site.
==Festivals== [[File:SaioMatsuri.jpg|thumb|The 2007 {{transliteration|ja|Saiō Matsuri}} in Meiwa, Mie Prefecture]] The {{transliteration|ja|[[Aoi Matsuri]]}}, the first of the three main festivals held in Kyoto each year, re-enacts the [[Heian period]] march of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} to the Shimigamo Shrine (lower [[Kamo shrines|Kamo Shrine]]) in Sakyo Ward. This festival is held every year on May 15 and in 2006 consisted of 511 people dressed in traditional Heian court clothing and 40 cows and horses, stretching around {{cvt|800|m}} from start to finish. This festival is said to have started in the 6th century when the Emperor sent his representatives to Shimogamo and Kamigamo Shines to pray from good harvests.
The {{transliteration|ja|[[Saiō Matsuri]]}} is held in the town of Meiwa, Mie Prefecture, on the first weekend of June each year. First held in 1983, it re-enacts the march of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} from her residence at Saikū, to the nearby Ise Shrine. More than 100 people dressed in traditional Heian-period dress along a section of the old Ise {{transliteration|ja|kaido}} (pilgrimage road), before ending in the grounds of the Saikū Museum.

{{Distinguish|Saiin (priestess)}} {{Italic title}} [[File:Saio.jpg|thumb|{{transliteration|ja|Saiō}} in {{transliteration|ja|[[jūnihitoe]]}}, 2007 {{transliteration|ja|[[Saiō Matsuri]]}}]]
{{Nihongo||斎王|'''Saiō'''}} or {{transliteration|ja|'''itsuki no miko'''}}<ref>{{cite book|title=スーパー大辞林|trans-title=Super [[Daijirin]]}}</ref> was the title of the unmarried female members of the [[Imperial House of Japan|Japanese Imperial Family]], sent to serve at [[Ise Grand Shrine]] from the late 7th century to the 14th century. The {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}'s residence, {{Nihongo|[[Saikū]]|斎宮}}, was about {{cvt|10|km}} north-west of the shrine. The remains of Saikū are situated in the town of [[Meiwa, Mie|Meiwa]], [[Mie Prefecture]], [[Japan]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.bunka.pref.mie.lg.jp/saiku/p0048200012.htm|title = 斎宮歴史博物館 Reduced-scale reconstruction of the Saikuryo}}</ref>
== Origins == [[File:Saio genji.jpg|thumb|left|image from the ''[[Tale of Genji]]'' showing what life at Saikū might have been like]]
According to Japanese legend, around 2,000 years ago the divine [[Yamatohime-no-mikoto]], daughter of the [[Emperor Suinin]], set out from [[Mount Miwa]] in [[Nara Prefecture]] in search of a permanent location to worship the goddess [[Amaterasu|Amaterasu-ōmikami]].<ref>Brown Delmer ''et al.'' (1979). ''Gukanshō'', p. 253; Varley, H. Paul. (1980). ''Jinnō Shōtōki,'' pp. 95-96; [https://books.google.com/books?id=18oNAAAAIAAJ&pg=PP9&dq=nipon+o+dai+itsi+ran#PRA1-PA10,M1 Titsingh, Isaac. (1834). ''Annales des empereurs du japon,'' p. 10].</ref> Her search lasted for 20 years and eventually brought her to Ise, Mie Prefecture, where the Ise Shrine now stands.<ref>''The Deep Purple Story of Meiwa (紫紺の語り部)'' (Meiwa Town Office, 2003), p. 3.</ref> Prior to Yamatohime-no-mikoto's journey, Amaterasu-ōmikami had been worshiped at the Imperial Palaces in [[Yamato Province|Yamato]].
According to the {{transliteration|ja|[[Man'yōshū]]}} (''The Anthology of Ten Thousand Leaves''), the first {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} to serve at Ise was [[Princess Ōku]], daughter of [[Emperor Tenmu]], during the [[:en:Asuka period|Asuka period]] of Japanese history. Mention of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} is also made in the {{transliteration|ja|Aoi}}, {{transliteration|ja|Sakaki}} and {{transliteration|ja|Yugao}} chapters of ''[[The Tale of Genji]]'', as well as in the 69th chapter of ''[[The Tales of Ise]]'' ({{transliteration|ja|Ise Monogatari}}).
In the 13th century, [[Jien]] recorded in the {{transliteration|ja|[[Gukanshō]]}} that during the reign of Emperor Suinin, the first High Priestess ({{transliteration|ja|saiō}}) was appointed for Ise Shrine.<ref>Brown, p. 253.</ref> [[Hayashi Gahō]]'s 17th-century {{transliteration|ja|[[Nihon Ōdai Ichiran]]}} is somewhat more expansive, explaining that since Suinin's time, a daughter of the emperor was almost always appointed as high priestess, but across the centuries, there had been times when the emperor himself had no daughter; and in such circumstances, the daughter of a close relative of the emperor would have been appointed to fill the untimely vacancy.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=18oNAAAAIAAJ&pg=PP9&dq=nipon+o+dai+itsi+ran#PRA1-PA9,M1 Titsingh, p. 10].</ref>
== Role == [[File:Saikū Historical Museum - Display item05 - The room of Saiô.jpg|thumb|Recreation of the room of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}, in the Saikū Historical Museum]]
The role of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} was to serve as High Priestess at Ise Shrine on behalf of the Emperor, to represent the role first set out by Yamatohime-no-mikoto. Three rituals a year were conducted at the Shrine in which the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} prayed for peace and protection. In June and November each year, she journeyed to the Shrine to perform the Tsukinamisai Festival. In September in the [[lunisolar calendar]], she performed the [[Kannamesai Festival]] to make offerings to the {{transliteration|ja|[[kami]]}} of the year's new grain harvest.<ref name="m9">''The Deep Purple Story of Meiwa'', p. 9.</ref>
For the rest of the year, the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} lived in [[Saikū]], a small town of up to 500 people approximately {{cvt|10|km}} north-west of Ise, in modern Meiwa, Mie Prefecture. Life at Saikū was, for the most part, peaceful. The {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} would spend her time composing {{transliteration|ja|[[waka (poetry)|waka]]}} verses, collect shells on the shore of Ōyodo beach, or set out in boats and recite poetry upon the water and wait to be recalled to [[Kyoto]].<ref name="m9"/>
== Selection process == When an Emperor died or abdicated the throne, when the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}'s relative died, or when certain political power required, she would be recalled to the capital and a new {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} selected from one of the new Emperor's unmarried female relatives using divination by either burnt tortoise shell or deer bones. The new {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} would then undergo a period of purification before setting out with her retinue of up to 500 people for Saikū, never to return to the capital until recalled by the next Emperor.
Upon the selection of the new {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}, the current {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} and her retinue would return to the capital to resume their lives as part of the Imperial Court. Often, a {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} was quite young when she left the capital for Saikū, and would only be in her mid-teens or early twenties when she returned to the capital. It was considered a great honor to marry a former {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} and her time at Saikū improved her own position at court and those of the people who served with her.
== Procession to Saikū == [[File:Saiku map.jpg|thumb|Map of the travel routes to Saikū, the seat of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}]] [[File:Tarumitongu.jpg|thumb|The Tarumi-tongū temporary residence]] The procession routes of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} changed after the capital was moved to [[Heian-kyō]] in 794.
The procession began in what is today the Arashiyama district on the west side of Kyoto. In the Heian period, successive imperial princesses stayed in the [[Nonomiya Shrine]] for a year or more to purify themselves before becoming representatives of the imperial family at the Ise Shrine.<ref>Kyoto City Tourism and Culture Information Site: [http://kaiwai.city.kyoto.jp/raku/backnum/dec07_e/buttone3.html Nonomiya Shrine.] {{webarchive|url=https://archive.today/20070626055413/http://kaiwai.city.kyoto.jp/raku/backnum/dec07_e/buttone3.html |date=2007-06-26 }}</ref> Contemporary annual processions recreate a scene from a picture scroll of the imperial court during the Heian period, starting from the shrine and continuing as far as the Togetsu-kyo Bridge, Arashiyama.<ref>Kyoto City: [http://kaiwai.city.kyoto.jp/raku/backnum/nov08_e/gyoji_dtle.html Saigū Procession];{{dead link|date=May 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} [http://raku.city.kyoto.jp/backnum/oct06_e/oct06_topics_e.html Events, October 2006.]{{dead link|date=May 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>
The procession of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} from [[Kyoto]] to [[Saikū]], the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}'s official residence in [[Ise, Mie|Ise]], was the largest procession of its kind in Japan for its time. Up to 500 people would set out from Kyoto as a part of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}'s retinue for the journey, which lasted six days and five nights. From Kyoto, they travelled in an eastward direction, passing through the [[Suzuka, Mie|Suzuka]] Pass, which was without doubt the most difficult part of the journey. Once clearing the pass, the retinue would descend into the Ise region and turn south, eventually reaching the {{nihongo|Kushida River|櫛田川}}. Here, the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} would stop to perform a final cleansing ritual before crossing the river and travelling the short distance to Saikū.<ref>''Saiō Procession'' (Documentary movie, Saikū Historical Museum).</ref>
The {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} was expected to remain at Saikū until the emperor whom she represented either died or abdicated the throne. The {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} was permitted to return to Kyoto only on the provision of a close relative's death. When returning to Kyoto, a different route was taken through the mountains to Nara, then to Osaka Bay where a ceremony was to be performed before she could finally return to the capital.
==From Japanese literature==
===Princess Ōku=== The {{transliteration|ja|[[Man'yōshū]]}} (''The Anthology of Ten Thousand Leaves''), tells the story of [[Princess Ōku]], the first {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} to serve at [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Shrine]]. The daughter of [[Emperor Tenmu]], Japan's 40th emperor (according to the traditional order of succession), Princess Ōku and her younger brother, [[Prince Ōtsu]], survived the [[Jinshin incident]]. After taking up her role as {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}, her brother was put to death for treason in 686 and Princess Ōku was relieved of her duties and returned to Yamato. Here, she enshrined her brother's remains on Mt. Futakami before she died the age of 41.<ref name="m6">''The Deep Purple Story of Meiwa'', p. 6.</ref>
===Princess Yoshiko=== ''[[The Tale of Genji]]'' tells the story of Rokujo-no-miyasudokoro, which is believed to be based on Princess Yoshiko, who served as {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} from 936 to 945. In ''The Tale of Genji'', Rokujo-no-miyasudokoro became the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} of Ise Shrine at the young age of 8, serving at the shrine for 9 years. After returning to the capital, she became a consort to [[Emperor Murakami]] and gave birth to Princess Noriko. She became famous throughout Kyoto for her colorful life, devoting herself to waka poetry and music. According to the story, she falls in love with Prince Genji, but her jealous nature brings about the death of two of her rivals. When her daughter is chosen as {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} at the age of 13, Rokujo-no-miyasudokoro decides to join her in Saikū to help her overcome her feelings for Genji.<ref name="m6"/>
===Princess Yasuko=== The love story of [[:en:Ariwara no Narihira|Ariwara-no-Narihira]] and the 31st {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}, Princess Yasuko (served as {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} from 859 to 876), is told in the 69th chapter of ''The Tales of Ise''. Ariwara-no-Narihira, well known in his time for his good looks, is married to Princess Yasuko's cousin, but on meeting at the Saikū, they fall into forbidden love. Giving in to temptation, they secretly meet under a pine tree on the shore of Ōyodo Port to reveal their feelings for one another and to promise to meet again the following night. But this first secret meeting would also be the last, as Narihira was due to depart that next day for [[Owari Province]]. Princess Yasuko came to see Narihira off, and they were never to see each other again, though it is said that Princess Yasuko bore a child as a result of the brief love affair.<ref>''The Deep Purple Story of Meiwa'', p. 5.</ref>
==End of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} system== It is not precisely clear when the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} system ended, but what is known is that it occurred during the turmoil of the [[Nanboku-chō period]] when two rival Imperial courts were in existence, in Kyoto and [[Yoshino, Nara|Yoshino]]. The {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} system had been in steady decline up to this period, with Saikū reverting to just another rural rice farming village after the system's collapse.
Though the area of Saikū remained, it was unclear exactly where the old Imperial town stood until pottery remains were unearthed in 1970 during the construction of housing in the Saikū area, Meiwa Town. A modern museum was built on the site of the first finds and archaeological excavations are continuing, held each summer with the aid of volunteer school children from all over Japan. Though a site for the main {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} residence has been discovered, a large percentage of it lies beneath the main [[Kintetsu Railway|Kintetsu]] Ise railway line and is inaccessible. Itsukinomiya Historical Experience Hall, a reconstruction of the building using traditional techniques, was built in the 1990s and stands beside Saikū station on the local Kintetsu rail line, no more than {{convert|200|m}} from the original site.
==Festivals== [[File:SaioMatsuri.jpg|thumb|The 2007 {{transliteration|ja|Saiō Matsuri}} in Meiwa, Mie Prefecture]] The {{transliteration|ja|[[Aoi Matsuri]]}}, the first of the three main festivals held in Kyoto each year, re-enacts the [[Heian period]] march of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} to the Shimigamo Shrine (lower [[Kamo shrines|Kamo Shrine]]) in Sakyo Ward. This festival is held every year on May 15 and in 2006 consisted of 511 people dressed in traditional Heian court clothing and 40 cows and horses, stretching around {{cvt|800|m}} from start to finish. This festival is said to have started in the 6th century when the Emperor sent his representatives to Shimogamo and Kamigamo Shines to pray from good harvests.
The {{transliteration|ja|[[Saiō Matsuri]]}} is held in the town of Meiwa, Mie Prefecture, on the first weekend of June each year. First held in 1983, it re-enacts the march of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} from her residence at Saikū, to the nearby Ise Shrine. More than 100 people dressed in traditional Heian-period dress along a section of the old Ise {{transliteration|ja|kaido}} (pilgrimage road), before ending in the grounds of the Saikū Museum.

{{Distinguish|Saiin (priestess)}} {{Italic title}} [[File:Saio.jpg|thumb|{{transliteration|ja|Saiō}} in {{transliteration|ja|[[jūnihitoe]]}}, 2007 {{transliteration|ja|[[Saiō Matsuri]]}}]]
{{Nihongo||斎王|'''Saiō'''}} or {{transliteration|ja|'''itsuki no miko'''}}<ref>{{cite book|title=スーパー大辞林|trans-title=Super [[Daijirin]]}}</ref> was the title of the unmarried female members of the [[Imperial House of Japan|Japanese Imperial Family]], sent to serve at [[Ise Grand Shrine]] from the late 7th century to the 14th century. The {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}'s residence, {{Nihongo|[[Saikū]]|斎宮}}, was about {{cvt|10|km}} north-west of the shrine. The remains of Saikū are situated in the town of [[Meiwa, Mie|Meiwa]], [[Mie Prefecture]], [[Japan]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.bunka.pref.mie.lg.jp/saiku/p0048200012.htm|title = 斎宮歴史博物館 Reduced-scale reconstruction of the Saikuryo}}</ref>
== Origins == [[File:Saio genji.jpg|thumb|left|image from the ''[[Tale of Genji]]'' showing what life at Saikū might have been like]]
According to Japanese legend, around 2,000 years ago the divine [[Yamatohime-no-mikoto]], daughter of the [[Emperor Suinin]], set out from [[Mount Miwa]] in [[Nara Prefecture]] in search of a permanent location to worship the goddess [[Amaterasu|Amaterasu-ōmikami]].<ref>Brown Delmer ''et al.'' (1979). ''Gukanshō'', p. 253; Varley, H. Paul. (1980). ''Jinnō Shōtōki,'' pp. 95-96; [https://books.google.com/books?id=18oNAAAAIAAJ&pg=PP9&dq=nipon+o+dai+itsi+ran#PRA1-PA10,M1 Titsingh, Isaac. (1834). ''Annales des empereurs du japon,'' p. 10].</ref> Her search lasted for 20 years and eventually brought her to Ise, Mie Prefecture, where the Ise Shrine now stands.<ref>''The Deep Purple Story of Meiwa (紫紺の語り部)'' (Meiwa Town Office, 2003), p. 3.</ref> Prior to Yamatohime-no-mikoto's journey, Amaterasu-ōmikami had been worshiped at the Imperial Palaces in [[Yamato Province|Yamato]].
According to the {{transliteration|ja|[[Man'yōshū]]}} (''The Anthology of Ten Thousand Leaves''), the first {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} to serve at Ise was [[Princess Ōku]], daughter of [[Emperor Tenmu]], during the [[:en:Asuka period|Asuka period]] of Japanese history. Mention of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} is also made in the {{transliteration|ja|Aoi}}, {{transliteration|ja|Sakaki}} and {{transliteration|ja|Yugao}} chapters of ''[[The Tale of Genji]]'', as well as in the 69th chapter of ''[[The Tales of Ise]]'' ({{transliteration|ja|Ise Monogatari}}).
In the 13th century, [[Jien]] recorded in the {{transliteration|ja|[[Gukanshō]]}} that during the reign of Emperor Suinin, the first High Priestess ({{transliteration|ja|saiō}}) was appointed for Ise Shrine.<ref>Brown, p. 253.</ref> [[Hayashi Gahō]]'s 17th-century {{transliteration|ja|[[Nihon Ōdai Ichiran]]}} is somewhat more expansive, explaining that since Suinin's time, a daughter of the emperor was almost always appointed as high priestess, but across the centuries, there had been times when the emperor himself had no daughter; and in such circumstances, the daughter of a close relative of the emperor would have been appointed to fill the untimely vacancy.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=18oNAAAAIAAJ&pg=PP9&dq=nipon+o+dai+itsi+ran#PRA1-PA9,M1 Titsingh, p. 10].</ref>
== Role == [[File:Saikū Historical Museum - Display item05 - The room of Saiô.jpg|thumb|Recreation of the room of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}, in the Saikū Historical Museum]]
The role of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} was to serve as High Priestess at Ise Shrine on behalf of the Emperor, to represent the role first set out by Yamatohime-no-mikoto. Three rituals a year were conducted at the Shrine in which the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} prayed for peace and protection. In June and November each year, she journeyed to the Shrine to perform the Tsukinamisai Festival. In September in the [[lunisolar calendar]], she performed the [[Kannamesai Festival]] to make offerings to the {{transliteration|ja|[[kami]]}} of the year's new grain harvest.<ref name="m9">''The Deep Purple Story of Meiwa'', p. 9.</ref>
For the rest of the year, the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} lived in [[Saikū]], a small town of up to 500 people approximately {{cvt|10|km}} north-west of Ise, in modern Meiwa, Mie Prefecture. Life at Saikū was, for the most part, peaceful. The {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} would spend her time composing {{transliteration|ja|[[waka (poetry)|waka]]}} verses, collect shells on the shore of Ōyodo beach, or set out in boats and recite poetry upon the water and wait to be recalled to [[Kyoto]].<ref name="m9"/>
== Selection process == When an Emperor died or abdicated the throne, when the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}'s relative died, or when certain political power required, she would be recalled to the capital and a new {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} selected from one of the new Emperor's unmarried female relatives using divination by either burnt tortoise shell or deer bones. The new {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} would then undergo a period of purification before setting out with her retinue of up to 500 people for Saikū, never to return to the capital until recalled by the next Emperor.
Upon the selection of the new {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}, the current {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} and her retinue would return to the capital to resume their lives as part of the Imperial Court. Often, a {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} was quite young when she left the capital for Saikū, and would only be in her mid-teens or early twenties when she returned to the capital. It was considered a great honor to marry a former {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} and her time at Saikū improved her own position at court and those of the people who served with her.
== Procession to Saikū == [[File:Saiku map.jpg|thumb|Map of the travel routes to Saikū, the seat of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}]] [[File:Tarumitongu.jpg|thumb|The Tarumi-tongū temporary residence]] The procession routes of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} changed after the capital was moved to [[Heian-kyō]] in 794.
The procession began in what is today the Arashiyama district on the west side of Kyoto. In the Heian period, successive imperial princesses stayed in the [[Nonomiya Shrine]] for a year or more to purify themselves before becoming representatives of the imperial family at the Ise Shrine.<ref>Kyoto City Tourism and Culture Information Site: [http://kaiwai.city.kyoto.jp/raku/backnum/dec07_e/buttone3.html Nonomiya Shrine.] {{webarchive|url=https://archive.today/20070626055413/http://kaiwai.city.kyoto.jp/raku/backnum/dec07_e/buttone3.html |date=2007-06-26 }}</ref> Contemporary annual processions recreate a scene from a picture scroll of the imperial court during the Heian period, starting from the shrine and continuing as far as the Togetsu-kyo Bridge, Arashiyama.<ref>Kyoto City: [http://kaiwai.city.kyoto.jp/raku/backnum/nov08_e/gyoji_dtle.html Saigū Procession];{{dead link|date=May 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} [http://raku.city.kyoto.jp/backnum/oct06_e/oct06_topics_e.html Events, October 2006.]{{dead link|date=May 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>
The procession of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} from [[Kyoto]] to [[Saikū]], the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}'s official residence in [[Ise, Mie|Ise]], was the largest procession of its kind in Japan for its time. Up to 500 people would set out from Kyoto as a part of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}'s retinue for the journey, which lasted six days and five nights. From Kyoto, they travelled in an eastward direction, passing through the [[Suzuka, Mie|Suzuka]] Pass, which was without doubt the most difficult part of the journey. Once clearing the pass, the retinue would descend into the Ise region and turn south, eventually reaching the {{nihongo|Kushida River|櫛田川}}. Here, the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} would stop to perform a final cleansing ritual before crossing the river and travelling the short distance to Saikū.<ref>''Saiō Procession'' (Documentary movie, Saikū Historical Museum).</ref>
The {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} was expected to remain at Saikū until the emperor whom she represented either died or abdicated the throne. The {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} was permitted to return to Kyoto only on the provision of a close relative's death. When returning to Kyoto, a different route was taken through the mountains to Nara, then to Osaka Bay where a ceremony was to be performed before she could finally return to the capital.
==From Japanese literature==
===Princess Ōku=== The {{transliteration|ja|[[Man'yōshū]]}} (''The Anthology of Ten Thousand Leaves''), tells the story of [[Princess Ōku]], the first {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} to serve at [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Shrine]]. The daughter of [[Emperor Tenmu]], Japan's 40th emperor (according to the traditional order of succession), Princess Ōku and her younger brother, [[Prince Ōtsu]], survived the [[Jinshin incident]]. After taking up her role as {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}, her brother was put to death for treason in 686 and Princess Ōku was relieved of her duties and returned to Yamato. Here, she enshrined her brother's remains on Mt. Futakami before she died the age of 41.<ref name="m6">''The Deep Purple Story of Meiwa'', p. 6.</ref>
===Princess Yoshiko=== ''[[The Tale of Genji]]'' tells the story of Rokujo-no-miyasudokoro, which is believed to be based on Princess Yoshiko, who served as {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} from 936 to 945. In ''The Tale of Genji'', Rokujo-no-miyasudokoro became the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} of Ise Shrine at the young age of 8, serving at the shrine for 9 years. After returning to the capital, she became a consort to [[Emperor Murakami]] and gave birth to Princess Noriko. She became famous throughout Kyoto for her colorful life, devoting herself to waka poetry and music. According to the story, she falls in love with Prince Genji, but her jealous nature brings about the death of two of her rivals. When her daughter is chosen as {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} at the age of 13, Rokujo-no-miyasudokoro decides to join her in Saikū to help her overcome her feelings for Genji.<ref name="m6"/>
===Princess Yasuko=== The love story of [[:en:Ariwara no Narihira|Ariwara-no-Narihira]] and the 31st {{transliteration|ja|saiō}}, Princess Yasuko (served as {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} from 859 to 876), is told in the 69th chapter of ''The Tales of Ise''. Ariwara-no-Narihira, well known in his time for his good looks, is married to Princess Yasuko's cousin, but on meeting at the Saikū, they fall into forbidden love. Giving in to temptation, they secretly meet under a pine tree on the shore of Ōyodo Port to reveal their feelings for one another and to promise to meet again the following night. But this first secret meeting would also be the last, as Narihira was due to depart that next day for [[Owari Province]]. Princess Yasuko came to see Narihira off, and they were never to see each other again, though it is said that Princess Yasuko bore a child as a result of the brief love affair.<ref>''The Deep Purple Story of Meiwa'', p. 5.</ref>
==End of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} system== It is not precisely clear when the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} system ended, but what is known is that it occurred during the turmoil of the [[Nanboku-chō period]] when two rival Imperial courts were in existence, in Kyoto and [[Yoshino, Nara|Yoshino]]. The {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} system had been in steady decline up to this period, with Saikū reverting to just another rural rice farming village after the system's collapse.
Though the area of Saikū remained, it was unclear exactly where the old Imperial town stood until pottery remains were unearthed in 1970 during the construction of housing in the Saikū area, Meiwa Town. A modern museum was built on the site of the first finds and archaeological excavations are continuing, held each summer with the aid of volunteer school children from all over Japan. Though a site for the main {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} residence has been discovered, a large percentage of it lies beneath the main [[Kintetsu Railway|Kintetsu]] Ise railway line and is inaccessible. Itsukinomiya Historical Experience Hall, a reconstruction of the building using traditional techniques, was built in the 1990s and stands beside Saikū station on the local Kintetsu rail line, no more than {{convert|200|m}} from the original site.
==Festivals== [[File:SaioMatsuri.jpg|thumb|The 2007 {{transliteration|ja|Saiō Matsuri}} in Meiwa, Mie Prefecture]] The {{transliteration|ja|[[Aoi Matsuri]]}}, the first of the three main festivals held in Kyoto each year, re-enacts the [[Heian period]] march of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} to the Shimigamo Shrine (lower [[Kamo shrines|Kamo Shrine]]) in Sakyo Ward. This festival is held every year on May 15 and in 2006 consisted of 511 people dressed in traditional Heian court clothing and 40 cows and horses, stretching around {{cvt|800|m}} from start to finish. This festival is said to have started in the 6th century when the Emperor sent his representatives to Shimogamo and Kamigamo Shines to pray from good harvests.
The {{transliteration|ja|[[Saiō Matsuri]]}} is held in the town of Meiwa, Mie Prefecture, on the first weekend of June each year. First held in 1983, it re-enacts the march of the {{transliteration|ja|saiō}} from her residence at Saikū, to the nearby Ise Shrine. More than 100 people dressed in traditional Heian-period dress along a section of the old Ise {{transliteration|ja|kaido}} (pilgrimage road), before ending in the grounds of the Saikū Museum.
